Container spot rates from Asia to the United States are easing after months of elevated pricing . SONAR data contributor Freightos (NASDAQ: CRGO ) showed Asia–U.S. West Coast prices down 6% this past week to $7,985 per forty-foot container. Asia–U.S. East Coast prices held level at $9,854 per FEU.
Port employers and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 watchmen reached a last-minute agreement Nov. 22. It averts disruption at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, but the deal is tentative until ratification. The union will keep working under its expired contract until it votes.
Daily West Coast rates are down to about $7,500/FEU so far this week. That is their lowest level since the end of August. East Coast prices have slid to about $9,000/FEU, back to July levels. Rates remain nearly three times higher than a year ago.
Several factors drove stronger-than-expected trans-Pacific volumes and an extended peak season. These included expectations of tariff increases, while weather-driven congestion and capacity reductions also helped keep rates higher even as demand cooled. Carriers are now adding blanked sailings as volumes soften and, with pre-Lunar New Year demand only a few weeks away, prices are likely to be quite elevated when they start climbing again.
Last week’s Trump-Xi summit ended with calls for stability in the trade relationship. China has since taken further conciliatory steps, including suspending some critical-material export curbs to the U.S. until January. Both sides are still preparing options ahead of the Jan. 10 trade truce expiration.
The Trump administration is planning to raise tariffs on goods from China by an additional 20% and hike import taxes on imports from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners. The proposals come ahead of the findings in a probe into excess manufacturing capacity expected as early as next week.
Several of the targeted countries have rejected the accusations. Freightos said the new tariffs would likely only restore duties to International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) levels, which the U.S. and its partners agreed to last year. It is unclear whether some countries will see that as escalation and retaliate.
Procedural steps would delay any new tariffs, and a comment period and hearings would likely take a couple more months. In the most recent Section 301 case, on forced labor, Trump enacted tariffs eight weeks after the USTR released its report.
Asia–North Europe prices dipped 1% last week to $3,374 per FEU. They have since climbed about $200 to $3,500 as carrier general rate increases push rates up despite a post-peak, pre-Lunar New Year lull. Asia–Mediterranean prices surged 20% to $5,162. Daily rates are up another $300 this week, though prices could backslide in the near term.
When Lunar New Year demand picks up, some forwarders expect existing congestion in North Europe to worsen. That would add upward pressure on rates, Freightos said. It could also lead carriers to start rolling — delaying or shifting — some contracted volumes again.
Why it matters: Falling trans-Pacific rates offer some relief post-holiday, but they are still nearly triple last year’s levels. Blanked sailings, Lunar New Year demand and the Jan. 10 trade truce expiration could push costs back up quickly.

The Concept 2032 E-Bike Is a Futuristic Spin on the Electric MTB Industry – in Line With Reality
11 photos
Photo: Victor Lucas
Bicycle design may just be one of the most explored of disciplines, next to cars, that is, and over the years, there have been countless ideas that have been brought to light. Some bicycle concepts are so well thought out that they even make it to production. The Concept 2032 isn’t an e-bike that’s yet available to the market, but is an exploration into what the future might hold and if it turns out like this, we’re in for some treats.
Victor Lucas envisions himself working for one of the hottest and fastest growing brands on the market: Amflow, and this concept takes a peek into the future, one that we may very well see become a reality in the next few years.
Photo: Victor Lucas What I loved most about the concept is that Victor took the time to research current and future trends in order to grant us a crystal ball image at what could very well be a reality some day. As mentioned, he chose the Amflow brand to build his concept around, and as such, there are a few things we can expect, and Victor delivers.
You may be aware that since 2024, when Amflow and DJI’s Avinox hit the scene, this brand has been focusing most of its attention on the full-suspension MTB scene, in the process, giving birth to e-bikes that compete with some of the world’s most established brands.
As the past couple of years have gone by, Amflow also saw its expansion into adventure biking, and most recently, the urban landscape. The latest bike is their UE Carbon , one that we’re currently testing, and if I may offer some short insight, is one of the most comfortable urban e-bikes I’ve tested in some time, if ever. All that brings us to the 2032.
Photo: Victor Lucas First and foremost, Amflow has made it their business to bring carbon fiber beasts to the market, and for this concept, that still seems to hold true, showing up to the stage with a smooth and weld-less look that is clearly poised for dominating the mountainside.
That frame is also designed around a XC-style top tube suspension with a rear action that’s built around a high pivot suspension, maximizing wheel travel and bump absorption while also granting the rider control over the while thing by placing you well within the wheels. At the front, Victor comes in with an inverted fork.
Yet, it’s not the suspensions and frame design that took my conceptual breath away, but rather, the attention to the drivetrain and battery that Victor has put into the design. As mentioned, this inspired human took the time to research what the industry currently offers and in the process, spun up his own ideas of what’s to come.
Photo: Victor Lucas Starting with the motor, Victor chose to go with an integrated motor and gearbox design and an eCVT transmission at the rear. Not only does this clean up the bike, but these days, it allows us to run setups that literally shift for you; just set the cadence and pedal away. Traction control is also part of this tech and Victor’s approach is one that’s in line with trends.
Personally, I’d say that the cycling industry is already here, and in a few years down the line, we may be seeing some other wild tech being adapted. I’m still waiting for someone to integrated a little generator and some software to manage power generation to potentially pedal on forever. Some brands have already played around with the idea. Schaeffler is one of them.
Then there’s the battery, a piece of the Concept 2032’s puzzle that’s sure to surprise you too. According to Victor, he foresees trends pointing to solid state batteries with lithium/silicon anodes, battery tech that’s meant to grant us access to packs that are half as small and twice as potent as what the market currently offers.
Photo: Victor Lucas According to his calculations, “ energy density is expected to be 400 Wh/kg .” If that holds up, we’re in for a real treat, especially if batteries like the 2032’s are to be available, not to mention mounting them the same way. Just look at how tiny they are.
With these batteries, Victor decided to eliminate the down tube integration of the packs and instead, mounts them right above the motor and BB. While the future of battery tech may not look quite like this, I personally love how Victor integrates his ideas of battery packs into the 2032. They look small, easy to use, and easy to swap. Picture having a couple of these in your backpack when you hit up the slopes.
Clearly, the Concept 2032 is just one possible route that the current bicycle industry can take, if ever, but that doesn’t change the fact that most, if not all that we see once started off as nothing but a concept such as this, a dream, if you will, and that alone can be seen as one of the driving factors of innovation, aside from necessity of course.
